title: Bridget of Sweden
hook: a widow, mother of a large family, founder, and visionary of the passion

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catherine of Siena, writing to the pope in Avignon. Your line was if you are what you should be. Did you send your honest letter? Day eight hundred thirty-two.
screen: `IF YOU ARE WHAT YOU SHOULD BE.`

segments.voice: What does a woman do when the life she built is suddenly over? In Sweden, a noblewoman has spent her married years running a household, raising a large family, serving at the royal court. Tradition says she and her husband went on pilgrimage together, and that not long after, he died. She is a widow now. Her children are growing up. She could step back into a quiet widowhood. Instead, her work is about to begin. She will found a religious order, travel to Rome and never really come home, and write down visions that people still read. Today: Bridget of Sweden.

Bridget, or Birgitta in Swedish, didn't become a nun and disappear. She became something harder to describe. After her husband's death, she gave herself to prayer, and visions came to her again and again. Her early biographers say she had one even as a child; now they filled her life. They kept returning to the passion of Christ: his suffering on the cross, and his mother Mary standing near it. Her visions were written down and gathered into books called her Revelations, full of the cross seen up close, painful and tender. She also founded a religious order, often called the Bridgettines, with a great house at Vadstena in Sweden. And like Catherine yesterday, she wrote to the popes in Avignon and urged them back to Rome. She went to Rome herself, lived there for years, and died there. One of her daughters, Catherine of Sweden, stayed with her and is honored as a saint too. The Bible pays particular attention to widows. In the Gospel of Luke, when the infant Jesus is brought to the temple, an old widow named Anna is there, and the King James Bible says she "departed not from the temple, but served God with fastings and prayers night and day." Widowhood, in that picture, isn't only loss. It can be a new kind of service. The letter of James is just as blunt about everyone else's part: "Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction". Catholics honor Bridget as a saint and a patron of Europe. Her life holds both sides: a widow's grief, and a widow's strength.
screen: `AN ORDER, AND A HOUSE AT VADSTENA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold a widow in mind. Bring to mind someone who has lost a husband or a wife. A grandparent. A neighbor. A friend's mother. Someone at church or work. It might be recent, or many years ago. Let their face come, and think about what their days are like now: the meals, the empty side of the bed, the quiet evenings. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If you don't, just hold them in your thoughts, with care. And notice if there's one small thing you could do this week: a call, a visit, a meal. The bell holds the time.
Bridget of Sweden. A widow and mother who, after her husband's death, founded an order, saw visions of the passion, and spent her last years in Rome.
Your line: a widow's strength. Today, make the call or the visit you thought of: to visit the widows in their affliction, as James puts it. Day eight hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Bridget of Sweden as a saint and one of the patron saints of Europe, and Bridgettine sisters still live and pray in houses that trace back to her order.

notes: Claims rule: the index hook's 'mother of eight' was softened to 'a large family' (the count is not in a cited text); the index is unchanged. Tradition gives eight children; a Keeper may restore the number with a source.

Biography (pilgrimage with her husband, his death soon after, her move to Rome, death there, daughter Catherine of Sweden, Vadstena, the Order of the Most Holy Savior, letters urging the popes back to Rome, co-patron of Europe) is standard but not in a cited text; confirm each.
'Many of them centered on the passion': the 'many' refers to her visions, not to a group of people; confirm.
'Write down visions that people will read for centuries' and 'lived there for years': soft time claims; editor may trim.
Original: χήρα (widow) in James 1:27 (χήρας) and Luke 2:37; confirm accent and pronunciation.
Editor: cut the sweeping 'by the standards of her time' claim; fixed the redundant carry and brought its James wording closer to the verse.

Editor (second pass): the myth item no longer says her life of prayer only began in widowhood (the teach says she gave herself to prayer then, not that she began); removed a doubled 'now' in the hook.

Auditor: the teach and myth said her visions began after Ulf's death; her Life records a vision of the crucified Christ in childhood, so the script now says the visions filled her widowhood and the myth is about the Revelations. The practice opened 'pray for a widow', which required prayer; now 'hold a widow in mind', with prayer offered as an option.
